clauses.reason: The only operative sentence of EO 8069 revokes the designation of Gateway, Montana, as a customs port of entry in Customs Collection District No. 33 (Montana and Idaho), and a second sentence makes the order effective at the close of business on March 31, 1939; the order is dated March 20, 1939. The revocation is self-executing: it needed no further act by an official, so the command was exhausted by performance when it took effect, recorded as 1939-03-31 (the close of business that day). The alternative reading, under which the designation lapsed only after March 31, would still place the effect on the next day, April 1, 1939. The surviving consequence is the removal of the port designation, a completed change and not a continuing command of this order.

research_rationale:
EO 8069 (March 20, 1939) revokes the designation of Gateway, Montana, as a customs port of entry under the act of August 1, 1914 (38 Stat. 609, 623), effective at the close of business on March 31, 1939. I read the held text of the Federal Register page (4 FR 1259) and compared the clause inventory with it: the order has one operative sentence and one sentence fixing its effective time. The held extraction also contains the Secretary of Agriculture's order suspending milk marketing Order No. 27, a different document; the dossier's wording signals about suspension and further order come from that document and not from this order. The revocation was exhausted when it took effect. No later instrument affecting this order was found in the held corpus. The held text is the machine-extracted text layer of the Federal Register issue; OCR wording remains subject to a page check against the PDF, which is not held.

savings.reason: The order has no savings or transition clause. The revocation changed the legal status of the port by ending its designation; that completed change, not any continuing command of this order, is the surviving consequence, and it is recorded as accrued. No held source shows any other residual effect.
